claims.text: Nobody will buy sgit because it is encrypted; if it succeeds it will be for better features, better workflows and a better solution, and leading with encryption was the author's own mistake.
claims.quote: I do not think anyone will buy sgit because it is encrypted.

claims.text: Innovation needs constraints and the loop of trying, failing and shipping, and the constraint that shaped sgit most was the encryption.
claims.quote: the constraint that shaped sgit most was the encryption

claims.text: The research is more careful than the slogan: a review by Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg found an inverted U-shaped effect of constraints on creativity and innovation, so some constraint helps and too much hurts.
claims.quote: an inverted U-shaped effect of constraints on creativity and innovation

claims.text: Encryption on the client moves the security problem from protecting all the data, every copy, backup, log and replica, to protecting the keys, which is a much smaller problem.
claims.quote: the problem moves to protecting the keys, which is a much smaller problem

claims.text: The sovereignty line stops being where the data is stored and becomes who holds the keys, so data can sit with a provider or in a country with sovereignty gaps and you can still move it.
claims.quote: The sovereignty line stops being where the data is stored and becomes who holds the keys.

claims.text: The European Data Protection Board's recommendations on transfers take exactly this case and conclude that strong encryption with keys retained solely under the exporter's control is an effective supplementary measure.
claims.quote: the EDPB considers that the encryption performed provides an effective supplementary measure.

claims.text: The memo said that with the data encrypted you do not have to worry about GDPR; that is too strong, and the article corrects it.
claims.quote: That is too strong, and the article should say so.

claims.text: For whoever holds the keys, encrypted personal data is still personal data: the UK regulator says not to think encrypted data is not subject to the UK GDPR, storing it is processing, and the controller's duties stay.
claims.quote: and that storing it is still processing. The controller's duties stay.

claims.text: The GDPR lists encryption as a security measure in Article 32, and under Article 34(3)(a) a breach need not be communicated to the people affected if the data was made unintelligible, provided the key was not lost with it.
claims.quote: provided the key was not lost with it

value.unit: GDPR article whose paragraph 3(a) lifts the duty to notify people when the data was unintelligible

claims.text: The European Court of Justice held in September 2025 that pseudonymised data is not personal data in all cases and for every person, which may help a store that never has the keys, but that store still processes data under a contract.
claims.quote: but that store still processes data on someone's behalf, under a contract

claims.text: The biggest gain is engineering: a server that cannot read the data removes both the possibility and the temptation of processing on it, so there is no server code, no complexity, no deployment, nothing to patch.
claims.quote: once nothing can run on the server, there is no server code: no complexity there, no deployment, nothing to patch

claims.text: sgit's server is, in the words of the first brief, a dumb key-value blob store, and the deployment is the client.
claims.quote: a dumb key-value blob store

claims.text: The author knows the temptation because he has fallen for it: a developer makes a change in the cheapest place, which looks like the server, until it has to be maintained.
claims.quote: I know the temptation well, because I have fallen for it.

claims.text: Some of sgit's most powerful features exist because the constraint had to be solved in version control: clone --path holds only the folders asked for, and with immutable encrypted objects a read is a plain GET any static host can serve.
claims.quote: With the objects immutable and encrypted, a read is a plain GET, so any static host can serve a vault.

claims.text: Open source is the second constraint: there is no private code, so the code is available everywhere and easy to deploy, run and change, including by the customer, which solves many sovereignty problems on its own.
claims.quote: The constraint is that there is no private code.

claims.text: Open source removes the temptation to lock the customer in; the best product is not the one you use because you have to but the one that hurts when you stop.
claims.quote: The best product is not the one you use because you have to; it is the one that hurts when you stop.

claims.text: The same is true of design: take things away until it hurts and stop there, because past that point it gets worse; sometimes that is one button and sometimes fifty.
claims.quote: take things away until it hurts, and stop there, because past that point it gets worse

claims.text: The curse of most startups is customers getting them to build features and integrations only they need until the roadmap belongs to everyone else; open source answers with the code, integrate it yourself or pay us for that thing.
claims.quote: here is the code; integrate it yourself, or pay us to do that specific thing

claims.text: You cannot open source half of it: a community edition that turns proprietary as soon as you use it for real is an evaluation version with a better name, and brings back every dependency open source was meant to remove.
claims.quote: A community edition that turns proprietary as soon as you use it for real is an evaluation version with a better name.

claims.text: Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis each moved to a licence that is not open source and each produced a well-funded fork, OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey; Elastic and Redis have since added an open licence back.
claims.quote: Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis each moved to a licence that is not open source

claims.text: Working in the open with no private code to protect and no lock-in to defend is more efficient, and is part of how very small teams can now build and maintain software that companies with billions cannot.
claims.quote: Working in the open, with no private code to protect and no lock-in to defend, is simply more efficient

claims.text: With the code open and the server holding nothing you cannot sell access to the code or rent the data back; what you can sell is customisation and keeping it working, which is the part worth paying for.
claims.quote: What you can sell is what the previous articles argued for: customisation, and keeping it working.

claims.text: Not that encryption removes GDPR: it reduces exposure, and the controller's duties remain.
claims.quote: It reduces exposure; the controller's duties remain.

claims.text: Not that constraints always help: the research says a moderate amount does.
claims.quote: The research says a moderate amount does.

claims.text: Not that small teams always win: it is the author's view from what he sees, not a study.
claims.quote: It is my view, from what I see, not a study.

claims.text: sgit's success is not shown here; the features are real and the market will decide.
claims.quote: The features are real; the market will decide.

claims.text: The author has a stake: sgit is ours.
claims.quote: I have a stake. sgit is ours.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo on 16 October 2026 whose GDPR claim is corrected here; sgit's facts are from the sgit-ai 0.22.0 code and changelog.
claims.quote: the GDPR claim in the memo is corrected here
